sec.title: Background
sec.p: Paramecia belong to the ciliate phylum of unicellular eukaryotes characterized by nuclear dimorphism. A diploid germline micronucleus (MIC) transmits genetic information across sexual generations. A polyploid transcriptionally active somatic macronucleus (MAC) develops at each sexual generation from a copy of the MIC through programmed DNA elimination (PDE) of > 30% of germline DNA. PDE requires the domesticated PiggyMac (Pgm) transposase. Assembly of Paramecium germline genomes has presented an enormous challenge owing to the difficulty of MIC isolation.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We report chromosome-scale short-read MIC assemblies for 7 species from the P. aurelia species complex. We discovered a novel clade of Helitrons, with 9–10-kb transposase ORFs under purifying selection, that have remained active in all P. aurelia lineages. A long-read assembly for P. tetraurelia together with a genetic linkage map provided a nearly telomere-to-telomere assembly.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The ~ 100-Mb genome consists of tiny (300 kb–1.2 Mb) and numerous (~ 160) germline chromosomes with the highest recombination rate ever reported for a eukaryote (420 cM/Mb). The ends of the chromosomes consist of Helitrons inserted in telomeric C4A2 repeats, forming a distinct genomic compartment that is eliminated very early during MAC development in a Pgm-independent manner.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The monophyletic Ciliophora, that emerged over a billion years ago [1], is comprised of highly diverse, very successful unicellular eukaryotes. Their most striking common feature is nuclear dimorphism, the separation of germline from somatic chromosomes in structurally and functionally distinct nuclei [2, 3]. Diploid micronuclei (MIC) ensure transmission of the genome across sexual generations but are not expressed during vegetative growth while a polyploid macronucleus (MAC) is responsible for gene expression. At each sexual generation, a new MAC develops from a copy of the MIC through programmed DNA elimination (PDE) that removes transposable elements (TEs) and their remnants and restores functional genes [4–6].

The first ciliate genomes to be sequenced were the somatic MAC genomes of Paramecium, Tetrahymena, and the distantly related spirotrich, Oxytricha [7–9], providing gene catalogs and information about MAC chromosome organization. The P. tetraurelia MAC genome assembly and annotations revealed a series of whole genome duplications (WGD) that occurred after the divergence of Paramecium and Tetrahymena (~ 500 MYa). Partially resolved by gene loss over evolutionary time [7, 10, 11], the most recent WGD occurred concomitantly to the emergence of the P. aurelia complex of at least 16 morphologically identical but reproductively isolated sibling species [12–14]. While paramecia reproduce sexually by conjugation of two cells with compatible mating types, the individuals from P. aurelia species can also undergo a self-fertilization process, autogamy, that yields 100% homozygous progeny [15].

The germline MIC genomes of only a handful of model ciliates have been assembled and annotated. The degree of fragmentation of the assemblies varies depending on repeat content and the feasibility of purifying the MICs [16–19]. The amount of eliminated DNA, estimated by comparison of MIC and MAC assemblies, varies from ~ 30% in P. aurelia and Tetrahymena to at least 95% in Oxytricha and P. caudatum [4, 14]. So far, the only model ciliate for which we know the number and overall architecture of the germline chromosomes with confidence is Tetrahymena thermophila [18]. Centromeric regions are found at the center of 5 large, linear germline chromosomes and most TEs are restricted to the center and the ends of the chromosomes. The assembly confirmed that Tetrahymena uses a specific 15 nt Chromosome Breakage Sequence to fragment MIC chromosomes during MAC development [18]. In striking contrast, pioneer cytogenetic studies in P. aurelia species suggested karyotypes with tens of small MIC chromosomes [20, 21]. Further, epigenetically determined fragmentation in Paramecium creates a variable set of linear chromosomes covering MAC-destined regions [6, 22–24]. Analysis of the variability led to the suggestion that MAC scaffolds could represent the arms of MIC chromosomes [24]. This “metacentric chromosome” hypothesis has been difficult to test for lack of knowledge about Paramecium centromeres.

TEs can affect host viability by disrupting genes or altering their expression pattern [25]. A remarkable feature of Paramecium and other ciliates is the way they control TEs. Epigenetic mechanisms, involving meiosis-specific small RNA pathways that guide histone modifications, silence TEs in Paramecium as in most eukaryotes [26]. However, in Paramecium and other ciliates, the process is taken to the extreme of their physical elimination from the somatic MAC genome. In the germline MIC genome of Paramecium, exons are interrupted by single-copy elements as small as 26 bp that are TE (Tc1/mariner DNA transposon) remnants known as Internal Eliminated Sequences (IES) [14, 16, 27]. Tens of thousands of IESs are precisely excised during MAC development, and time-course analysis of DNA elimination showed that IESs are eliminated earlier than TE or satellite sequences [28].

Elimination of IESs and most TEs and satellite repeats requires the domesticated PiggyMac (Pgm) transposase, which together with its Pgm-like partners, introduces DNA double-strand breaks at the extremities of IESs [16, 27, 29, 30]. This activity is tightly coupled to canonical non-homologous end-joining repair and gap filling of the cleavage sites [31–35]. Given the lack of a strictly conserved motif among eliminated sequences, how the Pgm excision complex is recruited to the boundaries of eliminated sequences is not fully understood. Data obtained so far indicate that all eliminated sequences do not rely on the same set of proteins for their elimination, suggesting that distinct yet partially overlapping pathways tether the Pgm excision machinery [36–38]. Indeed, most TEs and young, long IESs depend for their elimination on 25 nucleotide small RNAs, the scanRNAs (scnRNAs), whereas old, short IESs do not [14]. Initially produced from the entire MIC genome during meiosis by MIC-specific transcription factors [39, 40] and a dedicated RNAi interference pathway [37, 41–44], the scnRNA population corresponding to the non-eliminated sequences is subsequently degraded [44–46]. The remaining scnRNAs corresponding to TEs, in association with non-coding transcripts, then guide the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) to catalyze histone modifications on TEs in the developing MAC, providing specificity despite the lack of a conserved sequence motif [36, 38, 47–49]. It is then believed that these repressive histone modifications recruit or activate the Pgm excision complex [26], which, assisted by chromatin remodelers [50–52], triggers DNA cleavage at the boundaries of the eliminated sequences.

Purification of vegetative Paramecium MICs by a fluorescence-activated cell sorting strategy [16] was a tour de force given the MAC ploidy of ~ 1600n [53]: MIC DNA represents ~ 0.25% of total nuclear DNA, compared to ~ 5% in Tetrahymena. The first assembly using DNA from sorted MICs was fragmented (N50 ~ 37 kb) but adequate for confirmation that all IESs are retained when Pgm endonuclease expression is knocked down [16]. The assembly allowed genome-wide discovery of TEs, revealing 38 non-LTR retrotransposon families and expanding knowledge of Tc1-mariner DNA transposons to 13 families. A fraction (~ 3%) of the MIC assembly, enriched in satellite DNA but not in known TEs, was found to be eliminated independently of the Pgm endonuclease [16].

The present article describes the production of chromosome-scale assemblies of the MIC genomes of 7 species from the aurelia group. Our motivation was to understand chromosome organization in P. aurelia, determine the size and number of MIC chromosomes, identify and annotate repeated sequences, and provide reference genomes for functional studies. Efforts to obtain a telomere-to-telomere assembly for the P. tetraurelia model, using long-read technology coupled with information from a genetic linkage map, revealed the highest recombination rate ever reported in a eukaryote and a diploid germline genome consisting of ~ 160 pairs of small chromosomes. We discovered a new clade of Helitrons that have remained active in all lineages of the aurelia clade. Unlike previously annotated Paramecium TEs, most Helitrons are inserted in germline telomeres or sub-telomeric regions. Their elimination occurs earlier than that of other TEs and does not require the Pgm excision complex.

The six scaffolded assemblies have an average MIC genome size around 100 Mb (Fig. 1A), of which around 30% is eliminated during MAC development. With an average N50 of ~ 500 kb, these assemblies are of good quality (Additional file 2: Table S1). Indeed, > 99% of genes previously annotated using MAC genome assemblies [11, 14, 56] and > 97% of previously annotated IESs [14, 27] could be remapped to these assemblies. Analysis of the assemblies using the K-mer Analysis Toolkit [57] provided an assembly-agnostic assessment that the genomes are complete, with the possible exception of the P. sexaurelia assembly (Additional file 1: Figure S2).

The P. sonneborni genome is a case apart. Although scaffolds could not be built from the contigs for technical reasons (cf. Methods), the assembly (N50 ~ 33 kb) seems to be complete (Additional file 2: Table S1; Additional file 1: Figure S2). The assembly size of 217 Mb is at least twice that of the other P. aurelia MIC genomes (Fig. 1A), consistent with previously reported genome size estimates [14]. The large genome size is essentially owing to an increase of the MIC-specific compartment (the MAC genome size is ~ 82 Mb compared to ~ 70 Mb in the other aurelia species). Examination of the origins of the MIC sequences revealed that recurrent horizontal transfer of sequences from several other aurelia species can account for the increased genome size (see [58]).

sec.title: MIC genome content
sec.p: Paramecium MIC genomes consist of MAC-destined sequences (MDS) colinear with the corresponding MAC genome and MIC-limited sequences (MLS) that are eliminated during MAC development. To discover sequence features, especially within the MLS compartment, we used dedicated software to annotate genes, tandem repeats (satellite DNA), and dispersed repeats (TEs) for each of the 7 MIC assemblies.

Paramecium aurelia MAC genomes are at least 70% coding harboring ~ 40,000 genes of median size ~ 1.2 kb with tiny introns, separated by very short intergenic regions [11, 56, 59, 60] as shown in Fig. 1B. Given the demonstration that some functional cellular genes are partially or totally deleted in the MAC [14, 42], we looked for genes embedded in P. aurelia MIC-limited regions (Methods). The high MDS gene density sharply contrasts with the low MLS gene density that was found. Indeed, as shown in Fig. 1B, annotation of the assemblies detected a low density of 5–10% potential protein-coding genes (ATG … TGA, with or without introns), and an even lower density of potential non-coding genes (GC-content expected for coding regions but with no detectable ORF) in MLS. Moreover, the size of the ORFs in the MLS is significantly smaller than the size of ORFs in annotated MAC genes (Additional file 1: Figure S3A [11, 56, 58]; median sizes ~ 470 bp compared to ~ 1.1 kb), as expected for genes that have decayed (pseudogenes). The same trend is found in a comparison of non-coding genes, though the difference is smaller (Additional file 1: Figure S3A). Using RNA-Seq data sets available for P. tetraurelia [56], expression of annotated MLS genes was examined (Additional file 1: Figure S3B [48, 61]). Except for a handful of genes (n = 29 with RPKM > 1, top of heatmap), none of the 3257 putative protein-coding genes or 1177 putative non-coding genes appear to be expressed, neither in vegetative cells nor during MAC development. This suggests that they are mainly annotation errors or pseudogenes. However in cells depleted for Ezl1, the catalytic subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), a condition where TE expression was previously shown to be de-repressed [47, 48], the fraction of MLS genes that have transcripts (RPKM > 1 at T50) is larger (30%), showing they have the potential to be expressed.

To annotate satellite repeats, we combined two approaches, MREPS and TAREAN (“Methods”; Additional file 3). Minisatellites, mainly localized in MLS, represent only ~ 2% of the size of each Paramecium MIC assembly and ~ 6% of the MLS (Fig. 1B; Additional file 1: Figure S4). Minisatellite repeat units are generally species-specific, apart from minisatellites common to P. primaurelia and P. pentaurelia, the most closely related species (Fig. 1C, Additional file 1: Figure S5A). The large number of identified satellite repeats in P. sonneborni is very likely related to its large genome size. In order to see if the most abundant repeats are conserved across species, we sorted the units by abundance (Additional file 1: Figure S5B) and found that the most abundant units are not necessarily the most conserved. Since the diversification of the aurelia clade is relatively ancient (estimated 100–300 Mya) [10, 11], this is not surprising: rapid evolution of satellite repeats has been observed in other eukaryotes [62–65]. A notable exception is the 126 nt repeat (P126) similar to a WD40 repeat, the first Paramecium minisatellite identified because of its association with MAC telomeres [66].

Annotation of TEs (Methods) found elements from known superfamilies (LINE non-LTR retrotransposons and Tc1/mariner copy-and-paste DNA transposons) [16] and revealed Helitrons, DNA transposons that use a peel-and-paste mechanism of single-strand transposition [67, 68]. SINEs, MITEs, and uncharacterized repeats were also annotated. Despite the critical role of a domesticated piggyBac transposase in PDE, we found no traces of piggyBac transposons in any of the P. aurelia MIC genomes, in contrast with T. thermophila [18]. Surprisingly, although widespread in eukaryotic genomes, there was no hint of any LTR retrotransposons in these assemblies. LTR retrotransposons have not been found either in Tetrahymena thermophila [18] or the early-branching karyorelict ciliate Loxedes magnus [69], suggesting that these elements did not colonize ciliates.

The annotated TEs only account for ~ 5 Mb of the total genome size (almost exclusively in MLS), less than 20% of the germline DNA eliminated during MAC development (Fig. 1B; Additional file 1: Figure S4A). Overall, TIR (Tc1/mariner) and LINE elements were the most abundant (~ 2–3 Mb each) (Fig. 1D; Additional file 1: Figure S4B). Helitron occupancy varied across the aurelia clade, on average ~ 1 Mb (Fig. 1D; Additional file 1: Figure S4B). In the P. sexaurelia/P. sonneborni sub-clade, LINEs appear to be less abundant than Tc1/mariner TEs. This difference could result from invasion or proliferation of elements after the divergence of the two P. aurelia sub-clades.

We also used a guided approach to annotate TE protein domains for the purpose of reconstituting the evolutionary dynamics of Paramecium Helitron, Tc1/mariner, and LINE superfamily elements. We used Pfam domains specific for each superfamily to identify their occurrence in six-frame translations of the genome assemblies (Methods). The protein sequences of the least degenerate copies for Pif1 DNA helicase (Helitron), DDE_3 DDE endonuclease (TIR), and reverse transcriptase RVT_1 (LINE) domains were used to build phylogenies (Fig. 1E-G). The phylogenetic trees support ancient invasion of Helitron, Tc1/mariner, and LINE elements, pre-dating diversification of the aurelia clade.

Manual curation of the Helitron transposase ORFs was carried out for the 7 P. aurelia species. Remarkably, compared to curated LINE and TIR transposase ORF copies [16], a greater proportion of the Helitron ORF copies appear to be full size (Additional file 1: Figure S6). Conceptual translations of 112 full size Helitron ORF copies were aligned and used to build a phyML tree that identified 29 elements (Additional file 1: Figure S7A and B) [67, 70, 71] and has the same clade topology (A1, A2, and B) as the Pif1 domain tree (Fig. 1E). The analysis of synonymous (dS) and non-synonymous (dN) substitution rates showed clear evidence of purifying selection, with an average dN/dS ratio over all branches of the phylogeny of 0.15 ± 0.03 (see “Methods”).

A phylogeny of Helitron-like Elements (HLE) using the HUH endonuclease domain (Rep) [67, 72] and the Pif1-like helicase domain (Hel) [73] of Helitron transposases identified only two clades, HLE1 and HLE2, in the eukaryotic tree of life [74]. We added the homologous domains from curated Paramecium Helitron transposase ORFs (Fig. 1H). The Paramecium HLEs form a third, independent clade (“HLE Paramecium”) that is more divergent from HLE1 and HLE2 than the latter are from each other.

Intriguingly, Helitron ORFs are interrupted by up to 4 IES insertions in 9 of the 29 identified elements (8 from clade A2 and 1 from clade B), a frequency close to that observed for cellular genes. These IESs are generally conserved in all annotated copies from all species. One remarkable case is an IES inserted at the same site, in a conserved domain of the transposase, in all copies of 5 related elements forming a well-defined A2 subclade represented in all species (Additional file 1: Figure S7B). This IES insertion therefore likely became fixed in a common ancestor of the 5 elements before the beginning of speciation in the P. aurelia complex. In contrast to the flanking coding sequences, the IES appears to have evolved with almost no constraint, as previously noted for IESs inserted within cellular genes (Additional file 1: Figure S7C). Excision timing is similar to that of other IESs (Additional file 1: Figure S7D).

Even with improved annotation tools compared to the approach used previously for P. tetraurelia [16], a large portion of Paramecium MIC-limited genomes (50–70%) does not correspond to any annotated feature (gene, TE or satellite) (Fig. 1B). It remains very difficult to know whether regions with no annotation correspond to “dark matter,” i.e., sequence features no longer under selection that have evolved beyond recognition [75], or sequence features we do not yet know how to annotate.

sec.title: Counting chromosomes
sec.p: To determine the exact number of germline chromosomes, we generated a more complete genome assembly of P. tetraurelia using long-read sequencing (“Methods”, Additional file 1: Figure S1) and constructed a genetic linkage map, leading to prediction of the species’ karyotype. Because long-read sequencing library preparation requires more DNA than can be obtained from sorted vegetative MICs, we adopted an alternative strategy to enrich for unrearranged DNA. Pgm depletion does not prevent the elimination of ~ 3 Mb of MIC-specific sequence, enriched in satellite DNA [16]. We therefore used DNA from cells depleted of Ezl1, the catalytic subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) [36, 47, 48]. In this context, the additional 3 Mb of MIC-limited sequences, eliminated from PGM RNAi DNA, remain present [16]. However, ~ 33% of IESs (0.73 Mb; Additional file 2: Table S1) are excised [36].

Long-read sequencing of EZL1 RNAi DNA (1 M reads with a median size ~ 14 kb) enabled the generation of a high-quality de novo assembly (“Methods”, Table 1, Additional file 1: Figure S1B, Additional file 1: Figure S2, Additional file 2: Table S1). This assembly is less fragmented than the short-read assembly, contains the full gene complement, and retains 67% of IESs that escape excision under this condition.

sec.title: Construction of a genetic linkage map
sec.p:
To construct a genetic linkage map, we crossed strain 51 to strain 32, another homozygous strain of P. tetraurelia, showing 0.3% of sequence divergence in the MDS compartment, and sequenced the MAC of 39 F2 homozygotes obtained by autogamy of F1 heterozygotes (“Methods”; Supplementary methods in Additional file 4 [76–83]; Additional file 5: Figure S8A). We retained 220,994 biallelic SNP markers that we genotyped by mapping reads on the MIC assembly. In the absence of markers within MLS regions located at the extremities of chromosomes, crossovers (COs) could only be detected in the internal regions of scaffolds, consisting of MDS and IES regions (which altogether represent 70.9% of the MIC genome). In these regions, we detected a total of 12,206 cross over events (CO) in 39 meioses (313 COs per F2) (Fig. 2A&B; Additional file 5: Figure S8A-C). This corresponds to a recombination rate of 420 cM/Mb, a value that is extremely high compared to that found for most of the other species studied to date (Additional file 5: Figure S8D) [18, 84], and a genetic length of 31,000 cM, by far the highest ever reported (Fig. 2C).Fig. 2

In most eukaryotes, CO interference [85] constrains spacing of otherwise randomly located CO sites along chromosomes. We measured a 50% CO deficit at a distance of 22 kb comparable to that reported in S. cerevisiae (30 kb) (Additional file 5: Figure S8E) [86]. In general, the sequencing depth was uniform across all scaffolds of a given F2, which indicates that all MAC chromosomes have the same ploidy (estimated ~ 1600n in the MAC, vs. 2n in the MIC [53]). However, we observed that 8 F2s (21%) contained a few scaffolds (often only one) with a doubled sequencing depth over their entire length, indicative of MAC aneuploidy (Additional file 5: Figure S9). Similarly, using 74 independent published DNA-Seq datasets prepared from 100% homozygous cell lines, we found 21 additional cases of doubled MAC ploidy for 1 or more scaffolds (28%) (Additional file 5: Figure S9). These cases of doubled MAC ploidy most probably reflect MIC aneuploidy, resulting from chromosome segregation errors during meiosis (cf. Additional file 4 for further discussion). They occur with a frequency comparable to that reported in human (23.6%; [87]) (Additional file 5: Figure S9; cf. Discussion).

Analysis of linkage revealed that 37 P. tetraurelia contigs could be clustered into 17 linkage groups and that a few contigs consisted of two genetically unlinked segments, suggestive of chimeric assembly. We next constructed a composite genome, hereafter referred to as the “EZL1 assembly,” by integrating the linkage map to split or join the contigs into 187 supercontigs (N50 ~ 620 kb, 104.3 Mb). This assembly represents the closest proxy of the MIC genome currently achievable. It comprises 164 supercontigs (101.4 Mb in total) that encompass 166 MAC scaffolds, and 23 supercontigs (2.9 Mb in total) consisting only of MLS, for which genetic linkage could not be resolved. Notably, this assembly contains only two-thirds of annotated IESs, as the remaining one-third are still eliminated in Ezl1-depleted cells [36].

There is an essentially 1:1 relationship between the EZL1 supercontigs and the MAC scaffolds (Fig. 2D; Additional file 5: Figure S10; Additional file 6: Data S1). Indeed, the 164 supercontigs correspond to 161 supercontig “groups,” i.e., 158 supercontigs and 3 groups of 2 supercontigs linked based on the MAC assembly (Fig. 2D and Additional file 6: Data S1). Often, the EZL1 supercontig is at least twice as large as the MAC scaffold, corresponding to significant DNA elimination. More detailed analysis of the synteny between EZL1 supercontigs and MAC regions (Methods) showed that the sequences present in the EZL1 assembly that are absent from the MAC scaffolds are found primarily at supercontig ends but sometimes are more centrally located (cf. annotated Circos drawings: Additional file 6: Data S1). We conclude that the fragmentation sites used during MAC development are situated at the extremities of MIC chromosomes, although additional sites are sometimes more internal.

sec.title: MIC telomeres
sec.p:
The telomeres of eukaryotic chromosomes almost always consist of tandem repeats of a short, usually G + T-rich motif that is added by telomerase to the 3′ end of each strand. In the Paramecium MAC, telomeric repeats are a mix of TTGGGG and TTTGGG hexamers [88], the result of misincorporation at a single templating position in the telomerase RNA [89, 90]. In the EZL1 assembly, almost all supercontig ends are in MIC-limited regions (356/374) and many of them end with the same telomeric repeats as in the MAC (n = 135, Fig. 3A), suggesting they may be the telomeres of MIC chromosomes. To make sure they are not MAC telomeres that could have been added during MAC development in Ezl1-depleted cells, we used one difference between MIC and MAC telomeres: MAC telomeric repeats are added at variable positions following imprecise chromosome fragmentation [22, 23] during late MAC development (after 5–6 rounds of endoreplication, [28]), whereas the junction between telomeric repeats and adjacent sequences is expected to be fixed for MIC telomeres. We used high-coverage Illumina MIC reads [14] to identify telomere branch points, avoiding the high error rate and low coverage of ONT reads at supercontig ends. We selected reads containing a junction between telomeric repeats and non-telomeric sequences, clustered them and used multiple alignments to assess junction variability among individual reads of each cluster (Fig. 3B) (“Methods”, Additional file 6: Data S2). We were able to map 87% of these clusters to the EZL1 assembly (Additional file 6: Data S2 for details). As expected, clusters with variable junctions were found to represent MAC telomeres, in most cases (28/49) more than 50 kb away from the closest supercontig end (Fig. 3C).Fig. 3
P. tetraurelia telomeres. A Size of supercontigs containing MLS that are capped by telomeric repeats at both ends, one end or neither end. B Illumina MIC reads with telomeric repeats (mix of C4A2 and C3A3 hexamers) were clustered and aligned (Methods; Additional file 6: Data S2). Two categories of MIC junctions were found: MIC “edge” and MIC “internal,” in addition to MAC junctions. C Histogram (bin = 1 kb) of distances between telomeric repeat junctions and the nearest supercontig end, for each category. The last bin represents distances of 50 kb or greater. MAC telomeric repeat junctions can be detected in both orientations (black and white bars)

Among the clusters with fixed junctions, which are likely to be present as such in the MIC genome, a significant fraction (53/141) appeared to correspond to internal stretches of telomeric repeats flanked on both sides by non-telomeric sequences (the “internal” category in Fig. 3B-C) and therefore cannot represent the telomeres of MIC chromosomes. Nevertheless, they all mapped close to supercontig ends (max. distance 40 kb) (Fig. 3C). Intriguingly, they were all found to be in the same orientation, i.e., the orientation expected for a MIC telomere at the nearby supercontig end (CCC(C/A)AA near the 5′ end, TT(T/G)GGG near the 3′ end). As for the 88 clusters that have a single fixed junction and are flanked by non-telomeric sequences only on the 3′ side of CCC(C/A)AA repeats (the “edge” category in Fig. 3B-C), 75% of them (66/88) were mapped at the very ends of supercontigs. The remaining 22 turned out to be internal stretches of telomeric repeats that were not entirely included in the clusters of Illumina reads. Although this approach was limited by sequencing depth, we can conclude that the telomeric repeats present at 66 of the supercontig ends do belong to the MIC genome and are likely to represent the telomeres of MIC chromosomes. The size distribution of supercontigs that do not have telomeric repeats at their ends does not differ significantly from the size distribution of supercontigs that are capped at both ends (p > 0.09, t-tests, Fig. 3A). This suggests that the supercontigs could be quasi-complete and that P. tetraurelia has as many as 161 MIC chromosomes.

sec.title: Chromosome ends do not require Pgm for elimination
sec.p: The Paramecium germline genome is organized in distinct regions according to developmental fate. Constitutive MAC-destined regions are always retained in the new MAC and variable MAC-destined regions are partially retained via alternative elimination [14]. MIC-limited regions are eliminated during MAC development and include IES and OES (Other Eliminated Sequences) [91]. The question addressed in this section is where these regions are located on the chromosomes.

Genomic compartments were operationally defined using short-read coverage of DNA extracted from sorted nuclei: MICs, MACs, and developing MACs after PGM RNAi (Additional file 7: Figure S11; “Methods”). This is illustrated for one P. tetraurelia supercontig in Fig. 4A and drawings of all supercontigs are provided in Additional file 6: Data S3 and S4. Constitutive MAC-destined regions represent 70.2 Mb of the assembly, variable MAC-destined regions 9.2 Mb, and the MIC-limited compartment 19.9 Mb (IES 3.9 Mb, OES 16 Mb). The OES is further divided into a Pgm-dependent compartment (13.3 Mb) maintained in new MACs after Pgm depletion and a Pgm-independent compartment (2.7 Mb) first noticed by Guérin et al. [16], which is eliminated even upon Pgm depletion. Although considered to be a distinct compartment, all IESs are Pgm-dependent [16, 27].Fig. 4
Definition and characteristics of genomic compartments. A Genomic compartments defined by sequencing read coverage. JBrowse screen shot shows DNA-Seq coverage of a region of the EZL1 assembly by MIC, PGM RNAi and MAC Illumina sequence reads (top three tracks). MAC-constitutive and MAC-variable compartments are determined by a high and low MAC read coverage, respectively. The OES (Other Eliminated Sequence) regions were defined by no MAC coverage (IESs excluded) then divided into two compartments: PGM-dependent and PGM-independent, based on the PGM RNAi DNA coverage. See Methods and Additional file 7: Figure S11 for details. B Density of each genome compartment across assembly supercontigs showing their relative localization on folded chromosomes: 50% corresponds to the center, 100% to the ends. C Normalized DNA coverage (RPM) for non-overlapping 500-nt windows. The windows were separated into 3 groups, as a function of their compartment (MAC-constitutive, Pgm-dependent, or Pgm-independent). The boxplots summarize the presence of DNA of each compartment, for different DNA-Seq samples: sorted vegetative micronuclei (MIC), sorted parental old MAC fragments (FRAG), sorted developing MAC time course (DEV1—DEV4) at different ploidy levels (32C to 128 C) [28], and sorted or enriched (designated by a “*”) new MACs after gene depletion by RNAi; the samples are grouped by pathway (excision complex, scnRNA biogenesis and degradation, non-coding transcription, PRC2 components, and chromatin remodelers). These DNA-seq datasets are described in Additional file 8:Table S2

Figure 4B shows the relative position of each compartment calculated across all the supercontigs of the assembly. As in the example (Fig. 4A), the relative position of the MAC-constitutive compartment and of the IESs is greatest at the center of the supercontigs and vanishes towards the ends, while the PGM-independent compartment is restricted to the ends. MAC-variable and PGM-dependent compartment occupancy curves peak towards the chromosome ends but then decrease sharply.

Time-course analysis of DNA elimination using a previously published dataset [28] revealed that the Pgm-independent compartment is eliminated very early during MAC development, prior to IES excision and before the developing MAC reaches a ploidy level of 32C (Fig. 4C) [28]. To gain insight into the mechanisms of elimination of this compartment, we examined the consequences of depleting 32 known PDE proteins, by performing DNA-Seq of new MACs (see Methods) combined with analysis of previously published datasets (Fig. 4C, Additional file 7: Figure S11) detailed in Additional file 8: Table S2 [10, 14, 16, 28, 30, 33, 34, 36–40, 43–45, 48, 50, 51, 61, 91, 92]. As expected, the Pgm excision complex (Pgm, PgmL and Ku70/80c proteins) is dispensable for the elimination of this compartment. This is also the case for the chromatin remodelers ISWI1 [51] and Spt16 [50], which are required for IES excision. Given that the assembly was constructed using long reads from DNA of cells depleted for Ezl1, the catalytic subunit of PRC2, the Pgm-independent compartment is not eliminated in this condition (Fig. 4C). Unsurprisingly, depletion of other PRC2 components or cofactors (Eed, Suz12, Caf1, Rf2) also results in failure to eliminate this compartment. We note that two PRC2 cofactors, Eap1 and Rf4 [48, 49], appear to have a weaker effect compared to the other PRC2 components (Additional file 7: Figure S11). Depletion of the proteins required for scnRNA biogenesis (Spt5 [39]; Dcl2/3 [36, 37]), degradation of MIC-limited scnRNAs (Gtsf1 [45, 46]), and non-coding transcription (TfIIs4, [38]) showed they are important for its elimination as well (Fig. 4C, Additional file 7: Figure S11). Consistent with previous reports demonstrating that scnRNAs are produced from the entire MIC genome during meiosis [42, 44], the PGM-independent compartment is covered with scnRNAs (Additional file 7: Figure S12). We conclude that the elimination of the Pgm-independent compartment occurs very early during MAC development and involves the scnRNA and PRC2 pathways.

The next question is the localization of annotated sequence features with respect to the genomic compartments. A majority of TEs (75.3%) are in the Pgm-dependent compartment (Fig. 5A). More specifically, this is the case for TIR (Tc1/mariner) and LINE copies, while a majority of Helitrons are found in the Pgm-independent compartment. Consistent with the position of the different genomic compartments (Fig. 4), the Helitrons are overwhelmingly localized towards supercontig ends while LINEs and TIRs have a widespread distribution (Fig. 5B). Minisatellites are also widely distributed across all compartments, as illustrated by P126. However, some abundant minisatellites (CHBD0, SAT118, SAT189, SAT149, and SAT51) are exclusively present (> 90%) in the Pgm-independent compartment. As shown in Fig. 5C, SAT149 and SAT51 are located at the very end of supercontigs, while CHBD0, SAT118, and SAT189 occur near the extremity.Fig. 5
Genomic compartments and annotation landscape. A Barplots show the proportion of each annotated sequence feature (genes, TEs, and satellites) occupied by the 5 P. tetraurelia genomic compartments of the EZL1 assembly. The compartment occupancy proportion for each TE order (Helitron, TIR, LINE) and of the most abundant satellite families is also presented. The last bar shows the compartment occupancy of regions (n = 977) that have the potential to form G-quadruplex (pG4) and do not overlap telomeric repeats known to potentially form G4 (see Methods; Additional file 7: Figure S11). B Relative supercontig position of Helitron, TIR, and LINE occupancy on EZL1 supercontigs (as in Fig. 4B, the abscissa presents normalized distance to the nearest supercontig end). C Localization of the most abundant minisatellites on EZL1 supercontings (sequences in Additional file 3)

sec.title: Helitron insertions are restricted to chromosome ends
sec.p:
Helitrons are mainly localized in the Pgm-independent compartment (Fig. 5A&B). We looked more precisely at excision timing, excision requirements, and expression for each of the different Helitron copies with 9–10 kb ORFS (n = 79). The heatmap (Fig. 6A), showing sequencing coverage in different contexts, confirms that these elements are present in the MIC, absent from the MAC, retained upon PRC2 depletion, but for the most part are still eliminated upon Pgm excision complex depletion. As shown for the entire Pgm-independent compartment (Fig. 4C), the elimination of the majority of Helitron ORFs is sensitive to depletion of factors involved in non-coding transcription and the scnRNA pathway (Fig. 6A, Additional file 7: Figure S13). Helitron ORFs that belong to Clade A1 (Hel01, Hel03, Hel04, and Hel18) are eliminated early in new MAC development (before 32C endoreplication stage [28]). The other Helitrons are eliminated later, but earlier than LINEs and TIRs which are eliminated very late in MAC development (from 128C). Interestingly, some Clade A2 Helitrons (Hel09, Hel19), those that contain IESs and are retained after Pgm depletion, are also eliminated very late. Finally, some Helitron ORFs can be transcribed (Fig. 6A) as observed when Ezl1 or other PRC2 components are depleted (Additional file 7: Figure S13).Fig. 6

The phyML amino acid tree was made using MACSE to align the last 5000 nt of 79 full-length Helitron transposase ORFs, containing the conserved HUH Y2 (Rep) and PIF1 (Hel) domains (see Additional file 1: Figure S7A). We used this tree to define 5 Helitron groups (names of Helitron copies are found in Additional file 7: Figure S13). Clade A2 is split into 2 groups based on the presence of a conserved IES in Hel08, Hel09, and Hel19 copies (Group 2, red labels; cf Additional file 1: Figure S7) but not in the other Helitrons in the clade (Group 5, gray labels). The heatmap was made using DNA-Seq and RNA-Seq RPKM coverage after normalizing copies with respect to collapse (Methods). The 3 longest TIR and LINE copies were added to the heatmap for comparison. Samples used to calculate coverage are described in Additional file 8: Table S2. DNA samples from enriched but not sorted nuclei are designated by “*”. B Structure of some Helitron elements showing the position and orientation of the transposase ORF with respect to the supercontig end (on the left). Helitron Left Terminal Sequence (LTS) (green boxes) and Right Terminal Sequence (RTS) (blue boxes) were identified by manual alignment and curation. Satellites found between the LTS and the RTS are indicated by colored boxes. For the most abundant Helitrons (Hel01/15/16) the combination of LTS-satellites-RTS defines different “Types”. The presence of an IES is indicated for Hel09/19/08/17. The schema is not to scale. See Additional file 9: Figure S16 for more details. C Schematic representation of the Hel01Copy009 copy. ORF, LTS, RTS, and minisatellites are represented by colored boxes (green: LTSc, black: ORF, red: P126, orange: SAT54/81, blue: RTSb). In the zoom, flanking telomeric repeats (pink boxes) are found at both extremities (before LTS and after RTS)

sec.title: Structure of complete Paramecium Helitrons
sec.p: Helitron transposition involves nicking of the top strand at the 5′ end of a Left Terminal Sequence (LTS) which forms a covalent bond with the transposase, unwinding of the double-helix, and introduction of a second nick at the end of the Right Terminal Sequence (RTS), shortly after a stem-loop structure, to form a circular intermediate [68, 93].

To determine the full extent of transposable units, we looked for conserved terminal sequences marking the boundary with copy-specific flanks. We used DNA dot plots to compare ~ 50-kb genomic regions centered on the ORFs, for all copies of the abundant elements Hel01 (Fig. 6A clade A1) and Hel15/Hel16 (Fig. 6A clade B). Example dot plots between pairs of different copies of Hel01 are shown in Additional file 9: Figure S14. The ORF sequences present a continuous diagonal, surrounded by a variety of satellites that often differ in length among closely related copies (rectangles along diagonal) and are altogether missing in more distant copies (gaps in the diagonal). Alignment of the last 350 nt before the sequences diverge revealed 3 related consensus sequences, RTSa, RTSb, and RTSc, with a short stem-loop and ending with CCAA (Additional file 9: Figure S15A), an observation reminiscent of the CTRR found at the end of RTS in other eukaryotes [74, 94].

Similarly, RTSd and RTSe were found, by homology to RTSa-c, to end Hel03 and Hel04 (Fig. 6A&B). Alignment of RTSa-d consensus sequences and the unique RTSe showed characteristic RTS stem-loops with compensatory base changes, in support of this structure (Additional file 9: Figure S15A). The left end of the 10 Hel01 copies that did not extend beyond the end of the assembled supercontig (all Hel01 copies are oriented inwards from the end of supercontigs, see below) revealed a well-conserved LTSa sequence, which could also be identified at some supercontig ends in overhanging long-reads mapped with high confidence. The complete Helitron transposable units thus defined are schematically represented in Fig. 6C.

A similar analysis for the 15 copies of Hel15/Hel16 (Fig. 6A-B) revealed that most copies ended with an unusual Mosaic satellite (presented in detail in the next section; cf Fig. 7A) followed by one of several alternative RTSs (RTSf-m) that could be identified for 13 of the 15 copies (Additional file 9: Figure S16). The latter end with a CCAA motif, like the Hel01/Hel03/Hel04 element copies. At their left end, all 15 copies start with LTSb, homologous to LTSa, or a shortened variant LTSc (Fig. 6A,B, Additional file 9: Figure S16A).Fig. 7
Non-autonomous Helitrons and satellites of clade B Helitrons (Hel15/16). A Three examples of the structure of “Mosaic” satellite/RTS at the end of Hel15Copy006, Hel15Copy007, and Hel16Copy004. Each colored bar represents an occurrence of a mosaic repeat unit. The RTS are drawn as taller blue rectangles. B Three dot plots compare the Hel16Copy005 with itself, with a locus that contains a complete satellite array (right end of sctg002), and this locus with itself. The self dot plots show a square for each satellite, the non-self dot plots often show rectangles reflecting expansion or contraction of the number of repeats. To the right, a schematic comparison of the two loci illustrating loss of the ORF. C Similar comparison by dot plot (solid line parameters: > 70% ID, 28 nt windows) of two different supercontig ends (20 kb) each with a complete satellite array. “Y-tract” labels a stretch of at least 100 pyrimidines (C or T). D UpSet plot of the association of different satellites found at supercontig ends (n = 2 × 187), using the data in Additional file 6:Data S4. Each dot indicates the presence of one of the minisatellites. The barplot over the table shows their grouping in supercontig ends. The barplot to the left of the table shows the total occurrence of the different motifs. The black histogram bar shows the supercontig ends with a complete and ordered satellite array (LTSb/c, SAT149, SAT51, SAT41, Y_tract, SAT189, SAT118, and CHBD0). The gray bars show supercontig ends with a truncated and/or deleted satellite array. The very light gray bars represent cases that are difficult to interpret

Alignment of Helitron copies around LTS and RTS not only show that sequences diverge before LTS and after RTS, but also that there are C4A2 telomeric repeats before LTS and after RTS, suggesting that the copies may have inserted into the telomeric repeats. The example in Fig. 6C (Hel01Copy009) has a short run of telomeric repeats before LTSa and a longer run after RTSb. That this is the general rule was shown by alignments around all putative LTS (Additional file 9: Figure S15B) and RTS (Additional file 9: Figure S15C for clade A1 and Additional file 9: Figure S15D for clade B), whether or not they are associated with full-size ORFs (Methods). The LTSs are often, but not always, flanked by telomeric repeats that are at the very beginning or end of the supercontig (Additional file 9: Figure S15B). Remarkably, the RTSs are always followed by short stretches of telomeric repeats with the same orientation. This is particularly clear for RTSa-e associated with cladeA1 (Additional file 9: Figure S15C; see also Additional file 6: Data S4 scale drawings of supercontig ends).

In all cases where putative LTS and RTS sequences were identified, Helitrons point away from the chromosome’s end towards its central, MAC-destined region: LTS at the end, RTS towards the center. Interestingly, the orientation of full-length ORFs with respect to the orientation of the complete Helitron is variable depending on the element (Fig. 6B). In clade A1, the full-length ORFs are oriented in the same direction as the Helitron (except for Hel06), whereas clade B Helitron ORFs have the inverse orientation, pointing towards the chromosome end (except for Hel13). One way or the other, the orientation is always the same for all copies of each element (Fig. 6A&B, Additional file 9: Figure S16A, Additional file 6: Data S4).

The Pgm-independent genomic compartment is restricted to chromosome ends as are most Helitrons with full-size ORFs. Chromosome ends are also enriched in certain minisatellites (Fig. 5). We therefore used previous minisatellite annotations for P. tetraurelia (Fig. 1C, Additional file 1: Figure S5) and dot plots, which can reveal imperfect tandem repeats whatever their size, for each supercontig end (Additional file 6: Data S4) and each locus with a full-length ORF, to annotate the satellites within and around Helitrons. As shown schematically in Fig. 6B, the pattern of LTS-satellites-RTS for complete Helitrons differentiates sub-clades, hereafter designated “types.” Clade A1 contains 5 types and clade B, 3 types. Satellite annotations are drawn to scale with respect to all full-size ORFs in Additional file 9: Figure S16A. The manually curated Mosaic satellite that precedes the putative RTS of Hel15/Hel16 copies (Fig. 7A, Additional file 6: Data S3-S4, Additional file 9: Figure S16B) is unusual in that it is composed from 11 different ~ 44 nt segments with distinct sequences, assembled singly or as tandem repeats in an apparently random order. The generally low number of identical tandem repeats in this satellite made it difficult to detect with the automated pipeline (only the “Blue” repeat segment was detected, as SAT46). The Mosaic loci of Hel15/Hel16 copies all end with the “Red” segment and are followed at a short distance (42–168 nt) by the putative RTS (Additional file 9: Figure S16B). The near-uniform size of the repeat units and their amazing random assembly order raise intriguing questions about their origin, dispersal, and evolutionary history.

sec.title: Non-autonomous Helitrons are abundant at chromosome ends
sec.p: A search for LTS sequences in the assembly retrieved many copies not directly followed by Helitron ORFs. In the case of LTSa, 10 of them are followed by sequences very similar to the beginning and end of complete type 1 Hel01 copies, from which they may have been produced by recombination of two related satellites, SAT26 and SAT54/81, present 5′ and 3′ of the ORF (Additional file 9: Figure S17). These 10 LTSa-RTSa sequences, 6.5–9.9 kb in length, appear to represent type 1 Hel01 copies that have lost the ORF, as may also be the case for other, truncated loci. In the case of LTSb/c, 7 different satellites occur between the LTS and the ORF of Hel16Copy005 (Figs. 6B, 7B). The same array of satellites was found, without the ORF, at the ends of many supercontigs (Additional file 6: Data S3-S4; Fig. 7C). Their order from the end of each supercontig is consistent with the global analysis of satellite DNA distance from supercontig ends (Fig. 5C). Fifteen of the 62 complete copies that start with LTSb or LTSc, end with the Mosaic satellite and/or an RTSf-RTSm sequence (Additional file 6: Data S4). This suggests that the multiple copies of this satellite array may represent defective copies of the Hel16Copy005 type in which the ORF and in most cases the Mosaic-RTS are missing. Given the number of copies of this satellite array that appear to be complete, internally deleted or truncated (Fig. 7D), we estimate that at least 62 (complete arrays) and up to 196 (including truncated and internally deleted arrays) of these putative non-autonomous Helitrons have inserted at a chromosome end. The conservation of the order of the satellites in the array and of the unique copy sequences that connect them (Fig. 7C) suggests that a recent burst of transposition activity spread the arrays around the genome, after the divergence of P. tetraurelia from other aurelia species. Similarly, 20 other supercontig ends sharing blocks of P126 minisatellites between LTSb and Mosaic-RTS may be ORF-less derivatives of type 1 Hel15 copies (Fig. 6B; Additional file 9: Figure S18; Additional file 6: Data S4).

The annotation of full-length Hel01/03/04 and Hel15/16 elements indicated that they contain a variety of minisatellites which may have been dispersed at the ends of MIC chromosomes by transposition. The annotations further suggested that partial, non-autonomous Helitron copies lacking the ORF are much more frequent than full-length ones. If these characteristics hold for other Helitron families with fewer ORF copies, then a large fraction, if not all, of the Pgm-independent compartment would appear to result from Helitron-mediated transposition. To test this hypothesis, we made a compendium of Helitron full-size ORFs, RTS, LTS, and the specific satellites which may be assumed to be part of transposable Helitrons located at supercontig ends (50 kb ends; Additional file 6: Data S4). We found that 254 supercontig ends have Helitron annotations and 90% of these end in a Pgm-independent compartment, while 83% of the 74 extremities with no evidence of Helitrons do not end in a Pgm-independent region (Fig. 8A). A more chromosome-centric vision shows that the 161 chromosome-size supercontigs (Fig. 2D, Additional file 6: Data S1) usually have Helitron-associated annotations at one or both ends (both ends, n = 98; one end, n = 58; neither end, n = 5; Fig. 8B). The hypothesis that the Pgm-independent compartment found at chromosome ends results from Helitron transposition is well-supported by current data.Fig. 8
